finalText:
Five small files, wired into one thin request pipeline: `server.js` → `auth.js` → `routes.js`, with `routes.js` pulling data through `cache.js` in front of `store.js`.

- **`server.js`** — a plain `node:http` server. Every request first goes through `auth.js` to check the bearer token; unauthenticated requests get a 401 and never reach the routes.
- **`auth.js`** — tokens are `<userId>.<hmac signature>`, signed with a shared secret (`AUTH_SECRET` env var, defaults to `dev-secret`). No user database, just a signature check.
- **`routes.js`** — a small table mapping `METHOD /path` to a handler: `GET /users`, `GET /orders`, `POST /orders`. Reads go through the cache, writes go straight to `store.js`.
- **`cache.js`** — a 256-entry in-memory LRU with no expiry of its own.
- **`store.js`** — the actual data, held in memory, where each record expires 15 minutes after it was last written.

One thing worth knowing before you build on this: the route comment claims writes invalidate the affected cache keys, but `POST /orders` never touches `cache.js` — so a cached `orders:<id>` read can keep serving stale data even after a new order is written, until it ages out of the LRU on its own.
